newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: INTERVIEW - AAPT sees revenue growth/expansion.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW - AAPT sees revenue growth/expansion.

text.p: AAP Telecommunications Pty Ltd (AAPT), the third largest carrier in Australia but the least known, said its revenue growth would continue to soar ahead of the industry's deregulation next year and operations could expand beyond its business customer base.

"With deregulation there are a lot of opportunities such as residential that we might consider looking at. Even though today we want to remain focussed on the business sector," AAPT chief executive officer Larry Williams told Reuters in an interview.

However, AAPT, which is 51 percent owned by the Australian Associated Press (AAP) group, has no plans to build a competing national phone network with state-owned Telstra Corp and Optus Communications Pty Ltd.
The AAP group is controlled by newspaper publishers John Fairfax Holdings Ltd and News Corp Ltd.
Singapore Telecommunications Ltd owns 24.5 percent of AAPT, purchasing the stake which had formerly been held by the MCI group of the United States.
The other equal-sized stake is held by Todd Corp of New Zealand.

"The only way we would probably be able to compete in local (telephones) is for us to get in our own network and provide either a wireless interface or wire the customers ourselves and that is quite an expensive exercise," Williams said.

"It doesn't make sense even to have more than one network in the country and we are on our way to having three in Australia with two broadbands with both Optus Vision and Telstra building broadband networks and with Telstra's original copper network."
"So having a fourth is probably a real nightmare and is kind of crazy," said Williams, who first came to AAPT on secondment from MCI.
AAPT, which started as an internal network for the AAP group in 1985, expects annual revenue to continue to grow at a robust pace of around 100 percent in the 1996 year, Williams said.
"This year we are hoping to come somewhere close to A$375 to A$400 million," the American-born executive said.
This compares with annual revenue of A$200 million in 1995.

AAPT's revenue has experienced triple digit growth since its first started telephony services in 1991, when annual sales were around A$9 million, but Williams does not expect this rate of growth to continue forever.

"It is going to be very hard to maintain a doubling growth," Williams said. "We feel like we could grow A$100 million a year of new business, but that becomes a smaller percentage as you go down the road," he said.
The company's sturdy growth and the advent of market deregulation has had several stockbrokers knocking on AAPT's door offering multi-million dollar deals and float proposals.

"The opportunities that are coming across our desk are A$500 million or A$1.0 billion projects and as far as talking about those opportunities, we would need to look at bringing in either new partners or other ways to fund those kind of things."
Williams said AAPT has no bank debt and has A$80 million worth of equity.
He said the group has spent about A$80 million on telephony infrastructure and plans to keep annual capital expenditure at around A$20 million for the 1997 year.
"We do have some ability to borrow quite a bit of money from the banks and now we have enough cash to fund our normal capital requirements," Williams said.
